title: Non-Fiction Library
description: Explore real-world knowledge through child-friendly summaries of science, nature, technology, history, and biography.

books.title: How Your Body Works
books.summary: Your body is made of about 37 trillion cells, each doing a special job. The heart beats 100,000 times a day, pumping blood through 96,000 km of blood vessels. The brain has 86 billion neurons that communicate through electrical signals. Bones protect organs and make blood cells, while muscles work in pairs — one contracts while the other relaxes to move your limbs.
key_facts: 37 trillion cells in the human body
Heart beats ~100,000 times per day
Brain has 86 billion neurons
Bones make blood cells in their marrow
discussion: Which organ do you think is most important? Why?
How does exercise help your heart and lungs?

books.title: Life in the Rainforest
books.summary: Tropical rainforests cover only 6% of Earth's land but hold more than half of all plant and animal species. They have four layers: the forest floor, the understory, the canopy, and the emergent layer. The Amazon alone produces 20% of Earth's oxygen and holds 10% of all species on Earth. Deforestation threatens this vital ecosystem at a rate of about 1.5 acres per second.
key_facts: Rainforests = 6% of land, 50%+ of species
Four layers: floor, understory, canopy, emergent
Amazon produces 20% of Earth's oxygen
1.5 acres of forest lost per second
discussion: Why are rainforests called the 'lungs of the Earth'?
What can we do to help protect rainforests?

books.title: Mysteries of the Deep Ocean
books.summary: We have mapped only about 20% of the world's ocean floor — we know more about the surface of Mars. The Mariana Trench is the deepest point at 11,000 metres deep. Creatures like the anglerfish, giant squid, and bioluminescent jellyfish live in complete darkness under enormous pressure. The deep sea may hold hundreds of thousands of undiscovered species.
key_facts: Only ~20% of the ocean floor has been mapped
Mariana Trench: 11,000 m deep
More known about Mars surface than ocean floor
Deep-sea creatures create their own light (bioluminescence)
discussion: Why is ocean exploration important?
How do animals survive without light in the deep ocean?

books.title: Climate Change: What Is It?
books.summary: Earth's climate has always changed naturally, but since the Industrial Revolution, human activities have been releasing carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases far faster than natural processes can absorb. These gases trap heat in the atmosphere, causing global average temperatures to rise. Effects include melting ice caps, rising sea levels, more intense storms, and shifts in ecosystems. Solutions include renewable energy, sustainable farming, and reducing waste.
key_facts: CO₂ levels are higher than at any point in 800,000 years
Average global temperature has risen ~1.1°C since 1850
Sea levels rising ~3.6 mm per year
Renewable energy is the fastest-growing energy source
discussion: What changes can families make to reduce their carbon footprint?
Why is it important for countries to work together on climate change?

books.title: A Brief History of Time
books.author: Stephen Hawking
books.summary: Hawking explains the origin of the universe, black holes, and the nature of time for general readers — from the Big Bang to the search for a unified theory of everything.

books.title: The Selfish Gene
books.author: Richard Dawkins
books.summary: Dawkins argues that evolution works at the level of the gene, not the organism — genes 'selfishly' replicate themselves; also introduces the concept of 'memes'.

books.title: Cosmos
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.summary: Sagan's companion to his TV series is a journey through the universe — the history of astronomy, evolution, civilisation, and humanity's place in the cosmos.

books.title: On the Origin of Species
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.summary: Darwin presents his theory of natural selection — the mechanism by which species evolve over time through survival of the better-adapted — one of the most important books ever written.

books.title: Silent Spring
books.author: Rachel Carson
books.summary: Carson documents how DDT and other pesticides were destroying American bird populations, triggering the modern environmental movement and the eventual ban on DDT.

books.title: What Is Life?
books.author: Erwin Schrödinger
books.summary: The quantum physicist Schrödinger predicted that genes would be carried in an 'aperiodic crystal' — directly inspiring Watson and Crick's DNA research.

books.title: The Double Helix
books.author: James Watson
books.summary: Watson's personal account of the race to discover DNA's structure — candid and controversial, including his questionable use of Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data.

books.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
books.author: Thomas Kuhn
books.summary: Kuhn argues that science does not progress gradually but through 'paradigm shifts' — revolutionary moments when one world view replaces another (e.g., Copernican revolution).

books.title: The Ants
books.author: Bert Hölldobler & E.O. Wilson
books.summary: The definitive encyclopaedia of ant biology — 732 pages covering ant evolution, colony behaviour, communication, ecology, and interactions with humans.

books.title: The Code Book
books.author: Simon Singh
books.summary: A history of cryptography from Caesar ciphers to modern public-key encryption, including the breaking of the Enigma code and the rise of digital security.

books.title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
books.author: Richard Feynman
books.summary: Feynman's irreverent, funny memoir of his life — from cracking safes at Los Alamos to learning bongo drums — showing that great science and great fun are not opposites.

books.title: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry
books.author: Neil deGrasse Tyson
books.summary: In short chapters, Tyson covers the Big Bang, dark matter, dark energy, cosmic microwave background, and more — making cosmology accessible in under 200 pages.

books.title: The Gene: An Intimate History
books.author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
books.summary: Pulitzer-winner Mukherjee traces the gene's discovery from Mendel through the Human Genome Project, examining the ethical challenges of genetic medicine and editing.

books.title: Undeniable: Evolution and the Science of Creation
books.author: Bill Nye
books.summary: Bill Nye the Science Guy makes the overwhelming case for evolution through clear explanations, humour, and his famous debate with creationist Ken Ham.

books.title: The Emperor of All Maladies
books.author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
books.summary: Pulitzer-winning 'biography of cancer' traces the history of cancer from ancient Egypt through chemotherapy, gene therapy, and immunotherapy to today's breakthroughs.

books.title: Hidden Figures
books.author: Margot Lee Shetterly
books.summary: The true story of the Black female mathematicians at NASA whose calculations were essential for launching John Glenn into orbit — largely erased from history until recently.

books.title: The Body: A Guide for Occupants
books.author: Bill Bryson
books.summary: Bryson takes a fascinating tour of the human body — how it works, how it fights disease, and how remarkable it is that we survive at all, in his characteristic witty style.

books.title: The Soul of an Octopus
books.author: Sy Montgomery
books.summary: Montgomery's immersive account of her friendship with four octopuses at New England Aquarium reveals how alien yet emotional these intelligent invertebrates are.

books.title: How the Internet Works
books.summary: The internet is a global network of billions of connected devices. When you visit a website, your computer sends a request through your router to your Internet Service Provider (ISP), which forwards it across submarine cables and satellite links to a server that hosts the website. The server sends back data in small packets, which are reassembled by your browser. This all happens in milliseconds.
key_facts: Over 5 billion internet users worldwide
Data travels in small 'packets' across networks
Submarine cables carry 95% of international internet traffic
A single Google search queries thousands of servers
discussion: What would life be like without the internet?
How can we stay safe online?

books.title: Robots and Artificial Intelligence
books.summary: Robots are machines programmed to perform tasks. Modern robots use sensors, motors, and computer processors. Artificial Intelligence (AI) allows machines to learn from data and make decisions. AI powers voice assistants, self-driving cars, medical diagnosis tools, and recommendation systems. As AI becomes more capable, society must consider ethics: fairness, privacy, and who is responsible when AI makes mistakes.
key_facts: There are over 3 million industrial robots worldwide
AI can now beat world champions at chess and Go
Self-driving cars use cameras, radar, and lidar
AI diagnoses some diseases as accurately as doctors
discussion: What jobs do you think robots will do in the future?
Should AI always explain how it makes decisions?

books.title: The Innovators
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: The story of the digital revolution — from Ada Lovelace and Charles Babbage to Steve Jobs and the internet — tracing how collaboration, not lone genius, created the computer age.

books.title: Zero to One
books.author: Peter Thiel
books.summary: PayPal co-founder Thiel argues that the best way to build a company is to create something entirely new — going from zero to one — rather than competing in existing markets.

books.title: The Lean Startup
books.author: Eric Ries
books.summary: Ries argues entrepreneurs should use 'build-measure-learn' feedback loops to test ideas quickly and cheaply — pivoting when necessary rather than sticking to failed plans.

books.title: The Shallows
books.author: Nicholas Carr
books.summary: Carr argues that the internet is literally rewiring our brains for distraction — reducing our capacity for deep reading, contemplation, and memory.

books.title: Weapons of Math Destruction
books.author: Cathy O'Neil
books.summary: Data scientist O'Neil exposes how algorithms used in hiring, policing, and lending can entrench inequality and discrimination while claiming scientific objectivity.

books.title: Life 3.0
books.author: Max Tegmark
books.summary: MIT physicist Tegmark explores what artificial superintelligence would mean for humanity — jobs, weapons, society, and whether it would lead to utopia or extinction.

books.title: Masters of Doom
books.author: David Kushner
books.summary: The true story of John Carmack and John Romero, who created the video game company id Software and the games Doom and Quake — changing the games industry forever.

books.title: How the Internet Happened
books.author: Brian McCullough
books.summary: A narrative history of the commercial internet from the World Wide Web (1993) to the iPhone (2007) — the startups, gold rush, crash, and recovery.

books.title: The Art of War
books.author: Sun Tzu
books.summary: Ancient Chinese military treatise of 13 chapters on strategy, intelligence, and deception — now applied to business, sports, and martial arts worldwide.

books.title: Digital Minimalism
books.author: Cal Newport
books.summary: Newport argues we should radically cut our optional technology use and be intentional about which tools we use and why — reclaiming attention, solitude, and relationships.

books.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
books.author: Shoshana Zuboff
books.summary: Harvard professor Zuboff argues that tech giants have built a new economic order by harvesting human experience as raw material to predict and modify behaviour.

books.title: The Design of Everyday Things
books.author: Don Norman
books.summary: Norman explains why everyday objects like doors, phones, and kettles confuse us — and how good design should be so intuitive that failure is impossible.

books.title: Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution
books.author: Steven Levy
books.summary: Levy chronicles the original hackers at MIT in the 1950s through the PC revolution — exploring the hacker ethic of information freedom and hands-on experimentation.

books.title: Ancient Egypt: Land of Pharaohs
books.summary: Ancient Egypt flourished for over 3,000 years along the Nile River. Pharaohs were seen as gods on Earth and ruled a civilisation that built the Great Pyramids, invented hieroglyphic writing, and developed early medicine and mathematics. Mummification preserved bodies for the afterlife. The Nile's annual flood deposited rich silt, enabling agriculture in the desert. Egyptian culture spread widely through trade and conquest.
key_facts: Egyptian civilisation lasted ~3,000 years
The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BCE
Egyptians invented one of the first writing systems
The Nile is the world's longest river at 6,650 km
discussion: Why do you think the Egyptians built such large monuments?
What can we learn from studying ancient civilisations?

books.title: World War II: A Global Conflict
books.summary: World War II (1939–1945) was the deadliest conflict in human history, involving over 30 countries and causing the deaths of 70–85 million people. It began with Nazi Germany's invasion of Poland and ended with Allied victories in Europe and the Pacific. The Holocaust was the systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others by the Nazi regime. The war led to the founding of the United Nations and shaped the modern world order.
key_facts: 70-85 million deaths — deadliest war in history
Fought across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Pacific
Holocaust: 6 million Jewish people murdered
Led to creation of the United Nations in 1945
discussion: Why is it important to learn about the Holocaust?
How did World War II change the map of the world?

books.title: Guns, Germs, and Steel
books.author: Jared Diamond
books.summary: Diamond argues that geography and environment — not race or intelligence — determined which civilisations conquered others: Eurasian diseases, crops, and animals gave them an insurmountable advantage.

books.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: Harari traces humanity from the Cognitive Revolution 70,000 years ago through agriculture, empire, and science to today — arguing shared fiction is what makes us unique.

books.title: The Wretched of the Earth
books.author: Frantz Fanon
books.summary: Martinican-Algerian psychiatrist Fanon analyses colonialism's psychological impact on colonised peoples — arguing that decolonisation must be a violent rupture to rebuild identity.

books.title: The Silk Roads
books.author: Peter Frankopan
books.summary: Frankopan recentres world history around the Silk Roads — arguing that Central Asia, not Europe, was the real heart of global civilisation for most of history.

books.title: Annihilation of Caste
books.author: B.R. Ambedkar
books.summary: The undelivered speech in which Ambedkar, the architect of India's constitution, argued that the Hindu caste system was a fundamental moral evil that had to be destroyed, not reformed.

books.title: A History of the World in 6 Glasses
books.author: Tom Standage
books.summary: Beer, wine, spirits, coffee, tea, and Coca-Cola each defined an era — Standage traces how these six beverages shaped empires, revolutions, and global trade.

books.title: The Second World War
books.author: Antony Beevor
books.summary: Beevor's single-volume history of WWII places the human experience at the centre of the military narrative — from Stalingrad to Hiroshima — in vivid, multi-front detail.

books.title: Empire of Cotton
books.author: Sven Beckert
books.summary: Cotton was the world's most important commodity for 200 years — Beckert traces how its production through slavery and colonialism built capitalism and changed the world.

books.title: The Age of Revolution
books.author: Eric Hobsbawm
books.summary: Hobsbawm's classic history of the period 1789–1848 — the French and Industrial Revolutions — and how they together created the modern world.

books.title: A People's History of the United States
books.author: Howard Zinn
books.summary: Zinn retells American history from the perspectives of Native Americans, enslaved people, women, and workers — countering the triumphant narrative of presidents and battles.

books.title: Homo Deus
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: After Sapiens traces our past, Homo Deus looks at humanity's likely future — as we overcome disease, famine, and war, what will we do next? Become gods, or be replaced by AI?

books.title: The Clash of Civilizations
books.author: Samuel Huntington
books.summary: Huntington controversially argues that post-Cold War conflicts will be defined by cultural and religious differences between 'civilisations' rather than ideology.

books.title: The Black Jacobins
books.author: C.L.R. James
books.summary: James's history of the Haitian Revolution (1791–1803) — the only successful slave rebellion in history — and its leader Toussaint Louverture, who freed 500,000 enslaved people.

books.title: The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World
books.author: Fernand Braudel
books.summary: Braudel's masterpiece studies the Mediterranean Sea as a character in itself — tracing how geography, climate, and slow social forces shaped empires more than kings or battles.

books.title: Battle Cry of Freedom
books.author: James McPherson
books.summary: The definitive single-volume history of the American Civil War — placing the conflict clearly within the context of slavery, the Confederacy's commitment to it, and the Union's slow moral clarification.

books.title: Marie Curie: Pioneer of Science
books.summary: Marie Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish-French physicist and chemist who became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize — and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). She discovered the elements polonium and radium and pioneered research on radioactivity, a term she coined. Despite facing discrimination as a woman in science, she persevered to revolutionise our understanding of atoms and radiation.
key_facts: First woman to win a Nobel Prize
Only person to win Nobels in two sciences
Discovered polonium and radium
Coined the term 'radioactivity'
discussion: What challenges did Marie Curie face that scientists today don't?
How has her work on radioactivity helped medicine?

books.title: Nelson Mandela: Freedom Fighter
books.summary: Nelson Mandela (1918–2013) was a South African anti-apartheid activist who spent 27 years in prison for his fight against South Africa's system of racial segregation called apartheid. After his release in 1990, he led negotiations to end apartheid peacefully and became South Africa's first democratically elected Black president in 1994. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. His life is a symbol of forgiveness, justice, and peaceful resistance.
key_facts: Imprisoned for 27 years on Robben Island
Won Nobel Peace Prize in 1993
First Black president of South Africa (1994)
Apartheid officially ended in 1994
discussion: What does Mandela's life teach us about perseverance?
Why is forgiveness important in healing divided societies?

books.title: Long Walk to Freedom
books.author: Nelson Mandela
books.summary: Mandela's autobiography traces his childhood in rural Transkei, his transformation into an anti-apartheid activist, 27 years in prison, and his journey to South Africa's presidency.

books.title: The Diary of a Young Girl
books.author: Anne Frank
books.summary: Anne Frank's diary, kept during two years hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam, is one of the most powerful first-hand accounts of the Holocaust and a profound portrait of adolescence.

books.title: Steve Jobs
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: Based on 40+ interviews with Jobs himself, Isaacson's biography reveals the brilliant, often brutal creator behind Apple, Pixar, and the digital revolution.

books.title: Educated
books.author: Tara Westover
books.summary: Westover grew up in an Idaho survivalist family, never attending school, and taught herself to gain entry to Cambridge University — a memoir about the power of education to transform a life.

books.title: Becoming
books.author: Michelle Obama
books.summary: Michelle Obama traces her journey from Chicago's South Side through Princeton, Harvard Law, and the White House — a memoir of identity, ambition, and purpose.

books.title: Marie Curie: A Life
books.author: Susan Quinn
books.summary: A detailed biography of Marie Curie — the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences — examining her Polish origins, scientific breakthroughs, and struggles as a woman in science.

books.title: I Am Malala
books.author: Malala Yousafzai
books.summary: The Pakistani girl shot by the Taliban for campaigning for girls' education tells the story of her extraordinary courage, survival, and continuing advocacy.

books.title: Einstein: His Life and Universe
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: Isaacson's biography of Albert Einstein draws on newly released personal letters to trace the creative mind that produced the Special and General Theories of Relativity.

books.title: Man's Search for Meaning
books.author: Viktor E. Frankl
books.summary: Holocaust survivor and psychiatrist Frankl recounts his experiences in Nazi concentration camps and describes his development of logotherapy — the idea that finding meaning enables survival.

books.title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
books.author: Malcolm X with Alex Haley
books.summary: Malcolm X traces his journey from a troubled Harlem youth through conversion to Islam, rise as Black nationalist leader, pilgrimage to Mecca, and assassination.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
books.author: Frederick Douglass
books.summary: Douglass's first-person account of his life as an enslaved person in Maryland, his escape to freedom, and his emergence as the most powerful abolitionist orator of the 19th century.

books.title: Into Thin Air
books.author: Jon Krakauer
books.summary: Krakauer's account of the 1996 Mount Everest disaster, in which eight climbers died in a single storm — a gripping tale of ambition, hubris, and the mountain's deadly reality.

books.title: Wild
books.author: Cheryl Strayed
books.summary: After her mother's death and her marriage's collapse, Strayed walks 1,100 miles alone along the Pacific Crest Trail — a memoir of grief, recklessness, and radical self-discovery.

books.title: The Glass Castle
books.author: Jeannette Walls
books.summary: Walls's memoir of her unconventional, nomadic childhood with brilliant but dysfunctional parents — a father who promised to build her a glass castle but never delivered.

books.title: Mathematics Is Everywhere
books.summary: Mathematics is not just school work — it shapes everything around us. Architecture uses geometry to design stable buildings. Music uses ratios and fractions for rhythm and harmony. The spirals in sunflowers and nautilus shells follow the Fibonacci sequence. GPS uses trigonometry to calculate your exact location. Financial markets run on statistics and probability. Even social media algorithms use linear algebra to decide what you see.
key_facts: The Fibonacci sequence appears in sunflowers, pinecones, and shells
GPS uses 24 satellites and triangulation to find your location
Music time signatures are fractions (4/4, 3/4)
Encryption uses number theory to protect your data
discussion: Where have you noticed mathematics in everyday life?
Why is learning maths important for the future?

books.title: Fermat's Last Theorem
books.author: Simon Singh
books.summary: The 350-year quest to prove Fermat's deceptively simple theorem — that no three positive integers can satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for n>2 — finally solved by Andrew Wiles in 1994.

books.title: The Man Who Knew Infinity
books.author: Robert Kanigel
books.summary: The remarkable life of Srinivasa Ramanujan — an untrained Indian clerk whose letters astounded Cambridge mathematician G.H. Hardy with their extraordinary originality.

books.title: How Not to Be Wrong
books.author: Jordan Ellenberg
books.summary: Ellenberg shows how mathematical thinking — understanding sampling, regression, expected value — protects us from being misled by statistics, media, and our own intuitions.

books.title: Mathematics: A Very Short Introduction
books.author: Timothy Gowers
books.summary: Fields medallist Gowers explains what professional mathematicians do, how abstraction works, and why pure mathematics matters beyond its applications.

books.title: The Joy of X
books.author: Steven Strogatz
books.summary: Strogatz takes readers on a tour of mathematics from counting to calculus, group theory, and complex numbers — finding wonder and beauty in each topic.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.summary: Nobel laureate Kahneman describes System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, deliberate) thinking, and how cognitive biases lead us to predictable errors.

books.title: Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions
books.author: Edwin Abbott Abbott
books.summary: A Square living in a 2D world narrates his encounter with a 3D Sphere, using satire of Victorian social hierarchy to explain geometry and dimensions.

books.title: Things to Make and Do in the Fourth Dimension
books.author: Matt Parker
books.summary: Stand-up mathematician Parker turns geometry, topology, and infinity into approachable puzzles and activities — including how to fold a klein bottle or find prime numbers using a sieve.

books.title: The Sixth Extinction
books.author: Elizabeth Kolbert
books.summary: Kolbert reports from 12 different locations to document the current mass extinction of species — the sixth in Earth's history and the first caused by a single species: us.

books.title: The Overstory
books.author: Richard Powers
books.summary: Nine Americans, each changed by trees, are drawn together to try to stop the destruction of forests — a Pulitzer-winning novel that functions as an argument for tree consciousness.

books.title: Braiding Sweetgrass
books.author: Robin Wall Kimmerer
books.summary: Botanist and member of the Potawatomi Nation weaves together indigenous plant wisdom and Western science, arguing we should think of plants as teachers and partners.

books.title: The Uninhabitable Earth
books.author: David Wallace-Wells
books.summary: Wallace-Wells describes the worst-case climate scenarios if warming is not halted: heat waves, food shortages, pandemics, economic collapse — a stark wake-up call.

books.title: A Sand County Almanac
books.author: Aldo Leopold
books.summary: Leopold's month-by-month record of his Wisconsin farm develops into a 'land ethic' — the idea that humans must see themselves as part of nature, not masters of it.

books.title: The Hidden Life of Trees
books.author: Peter Wohlleben
books.summary: German forester Wohlleben reveals how trees communicate through underground fungal networks, raise their young, and help neighbours — challenging our image of forests as passive.

books.title: The Amateur Naturalist
books.author: Gerald Durrell
books.summary: Durrell's illustrated guide to observing and studying nature in your own garden, local woods, seashore, or urban park — inspiring generations of young naturalists.

books.title: The Story of Earth
books.author: Robert Hazen
books.summary: Hazen traces Earth's history across four billion years — from hot molten rock to the conditions that enabled life — showing how geology and biology co-evolved.

books.title: Feral
books.author: George Monbiot
books.summary: Guardian journalist Monbiot argues passionately for rewilding — returning wolves, beavers, and natural processes to degraded land to restore ecological richness.

books.title: The Republic
books.author: Plato
books.summary: Socrates and interlocutors debate the nature of justice, the ideal state, the allegory of the cave, and whether the just life leads to happiness — the founding text of political philosophy.

books.title: The Prince
books.author: Niccolò Machiavelli
books.summary: Machiavelli advises a new ruler how to gain and keep power — pragmatically, even immorally if necessary — in the book that gave us the word 'Machiavellian'.

books.title: The Second Sex
books.author: Simone de Beauvoir
books.summary: Beauvoir's founding feminist text argues that women are not born but made — that femininity is a social construction, and women must define themselves rather than be defined by men.

books.title: Discipline and Punish
books.author: Michel Foucault
books.summary: Foucault traces how modern punishment shifted from spectacle (public torture) to surveillance (the panopticon prison) — arguing power now works invisibly through institutions.

books.title: The Stranger
books.author: Albert Camus
books.summary: Meursault kills an Arab in French Algeria and is tried not for the murder but for failing to cry at his mother's funeral — Camus's novel of absurdism and alienation.

books.title: The Wealth of Nations
books.author: Adam Smith
books.summary: Smith argues that free markets, driven by individuals pursuing their own interests, generate wealth more efficiently than government planning — the foundation of modern economics.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.summary: Private reflections of the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius on how to live a good life through Stoic philosophy — duty, self-discipline, and accepting what you cannot control.

books.title: The Coddling of the American Mind
books.author: Greg Lukianoff & Jonathan Haidt
books.summary: The authors argue that well-intentioned 'safe space' policies are actually harming young people by shielding them from challenge — a polemic about free speech, anxiety, and fragility.

books.title: Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?
books.author: Michael Sandel
books.summary: Harvard professor Sandel's accessible introduction to moral philosophy — using dilemmas from trolley problems to Afghanistan to explore utilitarianism, Kant, and Rawls.

books.title: The Tipping Point
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Gladwell argues that ideas, trends, and social change spread like epidemics — and that small factors can cause a sudden tipping point when change becomes unstoppable.

books.title: Freakonomics
books.author: Steven Levitt & Stephen Dubner
books.summary: An economist and journalist apply economic thinking to unexpected questions: What do drug dealers and sumo wrestlers have in common? Why did US crime fall in the 1990s?

books.title: The Art of Happiness
books.author: Dalai Lama & Howard Cutler
books.summary: Psychiatrist Cutler interviews the Dalai Lama about happiness across multiple sessions, drawing on both Buddhist wisdom and Western psychology to define what happiness actually is.

books.title: A Brief History of Time
books.author: Stephen Hawking
books.summary: Stephen Hawking explains the universe's most profound mysteries—black holes, the Big Bang, the nature of time—in language accessible to non-scientists. This bestseller changed how the public thinks about cosmology and inspired millions to look up at the stars.
key_ideas: Time has a beginning (the Big Bang)
Black holes are regions where gravity is so strong even light cannot escape
The universe began 13.8 billion years ago
key_facts: The observable universe is 93 billion light-years across
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth
Light from the sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth
discussion: What is a black hole?
Do you think the universe had a beginning?

books.title: The Planets
books.author: Dava Sobel
books.summary: Sobel weaves together mythology, science, and literature to tell the story of each planet in our solar system. Mixing history and cutting-edge planetary science, she reveals each world's unique character through the lens of human culture.
key_ideas: Each planet has its own unique characteristics and history
Planets were named after Roman gods
Space exploration has revealed surprising worlds
key_facts: Jupiter is large enough to contain all other planets combined
Venus is the hottest planet despite not being closest to the sun
Saturn's rings are mostly water ice
discussion: Which planet would you most want to visit?
How has our understanding of the solar system changed?

books.title: Cosmos
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.summary: Carl Sagan's companion to his landmark TV series explores 15 billion years of cosmic evolution, from the Big Bang to the present. Written with poetic awe and scientific rigor, it argues that understanding the cosmos is essential to understanding ourselves.
key_ideas: We are made of starstuff—the atoms in our bodies were forged in stars
The Milky Way contains 200-400 billion stars
Science is a way of thinking, not just a collection of facts
key_facts: Carl Sagan coined the phrase 'billions and billions'
The cosmic calendar compresses all of history into one year
Voyager 1 is now over 23 billion km from the Sun
discussion: What does 'we are starstuff' mean?
Why does Sagan call Earth a 'pale blue dot'?

books.title: Space Exploration A History
books.author: John Catchpole
books.summary: A comprehensive history of humanity's ventures into space, from the earliest rockets through Apollo, Skylab, the Space Shuttle, and the International Space Station. Includes detailed accounts of both triumphs and tragedies.
key_ideas: Spaceflight requires solving problems of propulsion, life support, and re-entry
International cooperation has expanded human presence in space
Each mission built on lessons from previous ones
key_facts: Yuri Gagarin was the first human in space (April 12, 1961)
